title: AI-Ready Logistics Stack: 12 Critical Components Audit
subtitle: For operations leaders at 50-200 employee logistics firms. Score your stack against the 12 components that decide whether agentic automation lands or leaks.

benchmarks.metric: Delivery effectiveness lift from AI document validation (Domina case)
Real-time data access improvement after unified event stream (Domina case)

methodology_anchor.name: Agent-Ready Ops
preconditions: Structured input data. Your shipment, document, and event sources are clean enough to be the input layer for an automated decision.
Documentable decision logic. The rules your senior dispatchers and ops leads follow can be written down explicitly.
Narrow initial scope. The first cut handles a single decision in a single workflow, not the whole dispatch floor.
Human-in-the-loop by design. Every agent output touches a dispatcher, ops lead, or compliance reviewer before it ships externally.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores your logistics stack against the four preconditions for Agent-Ready Ops. Hit all four and the workflow is ready for AI to carry weight. Miss one and any AI build will leak six weeks in.

proof_card.sample_top_leak: shipment status reconciliation across TMS, WMS, and carrier APIs (~18 hrs/week of dispatcher rework)

persona_selector.text: Which best describes your logistics operation?

answers.label: Under 50 employees, single facility
50-100 employees, 1-2 facilities
101-200 employees, multi-facility or multi-mode
200+ employees, regional or national network

questions.text: How consistently do you have a single source of truth for shipment status across TMS, WMS, and carrier APIs?

answers.label: 1. Status lives in 3+ systems, reconciled nightly or by hand
2. One primary system but dispatchers cross-check 2 others daily
3. System of record exists but carrier APIs lag by hours
4. Single source of truth, near real-time sync, occasional drift
5. Unified status layer, sub-minute sync, agents can trust it

questions.text: How structured is your shipment order intake (addresses, weights, dimensions, special handling)?

answers.label: 1. Free-text fields everywhere, optional weight, no validation
2. Some structured fields but free-text addresses are common
3. Most fields structured, validation on critical ones, gaps remain
4. Fully structured intake, address verification, required dims and weight
5. Structured intake with API-enforced schemas, zero free-text on routing fields

questions.text: How real-time is your event stream from scanners, GPS, and POD devices into a single warehouse?

answers.label: 1. Events live in device-specific silos, pulled into reports weekly
2. Daily batch loads into a warehouse, no real-time path
3. Hourly loads, partial coverage of scanner and GPS sources
4. Near real-time stream, most sources unified, gaps on POD
5. Full real-time event stream, all device classes feeding one warehouse

questions.text: How queryable is your historical shipment data (24+ months) for pattern analysis?

answers.label: 1. Most history archived in PDFs or carrier portals, not queryable
2. 6-12 months queryable, older data in PDFs or flat files
3. 24 months queryable but spread across systems, no unified schema
4. 24+ months in a warehouse, unified schema, dispatchers can self-serve
5. 36+ months queryable, clean schema, ready for return prediction and routing models

low.headline: Your data foundation will sink any AI build
low.text: Status spread across 3 systems, free-text addresses, and PDF-archived history mean any agent you wire in will hallucinate ETAs by the second shift. Fix the foundation before the model.
steps: Pick one system as the shipment status source of truth and write the reconciliation rules between it and the other two
Lock down structured intake on the 5 fields that drive routing: origin, destination, weight, dims, handling code
Stand up a single warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, or Supabase) and pipe scanner + GPS + POD events into it before touching any AI

mid.headline: Foundation is partial, agents will work then break
mid.text: You have a system of record but carrier APIs lag, and your event stream has coverage gaps. Agents will run fine on the happy path and fail on the 20% of shipments that touch the gap.
steps: Close the carrier API sync lag to under 15 minutes for tier-1 carriers
Map every event source (scanners, GPS, POD, customs) and identify the 1-2 still loading in batch, move them to streaming
Migrate the last archived historical year out of PDFs into the warehouse so return-pattern queries work

high.headline: Foundation is ready, agents can carry weight
high.text: Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add data quality monitoring on the event stream, alert on schema drift before agents see bad input
Run a 90-day return prediction model on your historical warehouse, see if the pattern depth holds up
Document data contracts between TMS, WMS, and the warehouse so vendor swaps don't break agents downstream

operator_brief.headline_number: ~18 hrs/week of dispatcher rework recoverable from a single source of truth
operator_brief.lever: Pick the system of record for shipment status this quarter and stop the nightly reconciliation game.
talking_points: Every hour a dispatcher spends cross-checking status across TMS, WMS, and carrier portals is an hour they're not exception-managing
The 80% real-time data access lift in the Domina case happened because the event stream existed before AI was added, not after
Free-text address fields are the single biggest source of routing failure when agents take over dispatch decisions
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, instrument shipment status reconciliation time across your top 3 dispatchers and quantify weekly hours lost to cross-system lookups.

questions.text: How automated is OCR capture for BOLs, PODs, customs forms, and damage reports?

answers.label: 1. Documents are scanned and filed, no OCR, ops keys data manually
2. Basic OCR on BOLs only, everything else manual
3. OCR on BOLs and PODs, customs and damage still manual
4. OCR across all 4 doc types, human review on exceptions
5. OCR + structured extraction across all doc types, agents validate against shipment record

questions.text: How automated is the validation of document data against the shipment record?

answers.label: 1. No automated validation, mismatches caught at billing or audit
2. Manual spot-checks by ops on high-value shipments
3. Rules engine flags mismatches on weight or count, rest is manual
4. Validation across most fields, ops reviews flagged exceptions
5. Full doc-to-record validation, agents auto-resolve clean matches, route exceptions

questions.text: How structured is the routing of doc exceptions to the right human reviewer?

answers.label: 1. Exceptions pile up in an inbox, anyone with time grabs one
2. Manual triage by an ops coordinator each morning
3. Basic routing rules by doc type, no SLA tracking
4. Routing by doc type + value + customer tier, SLAs tracked
5. Auto-routing by 5+ attributes, SLA dashboard, escalation paths defined

low.headline: Document layer is keying data your stack should be reading
low.text: Manual keying of BOLs and PODs is the most visible leak in a 50-200 person op. Domina's 15% delivery effectiveness lift came from this layer specifically.
steps: Pick the highest-volume doc type (usually BOL or POD) and stand up OCR + structured extraction in one week
Write the validation rules between extracted doc data and shipment record, weight + count + address are table stakes
Define the exception inbox owner and the SLA before any agent is wired in

mid.headline: Doc capture works, validation is the gap
mid.text: You're capturing data but not validating it against the shipment record automatically. That gap is where the billing disputes and damage claims hide.
steps: Extend validation rules to all 4 doc types: BOL, POD, customs, damage
Build the exception routing logic by customer tier and dollar value, not just doc type
Track SLA on exception resolution weekly, surface the recurring failure modes to ops leadership

high.headline: Doc layer is agent-ready
high.text: Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add agent-driven auto-resolution on clean matches above 95% confidence, route the rest
Instrument confidence-score drift over time, retrain or retune when accuracy slips
Pipe validation outcomes into your shipment record so downstream agents inherit the audit trail

operator_brief.headline_number: ~22 hrs/week of manual doc keying and validation recoverable
operator_brief.lever: Wire OCR + structured extraction into your highest-volume doc type this quarter before adding any predictive AI.
talking_points: Domina's 15% delivery effectiveness lift came from AI doc validation, the doc layer is the highest-ROI starting point
Manual doc keying is where billing errors and damage claim disputes originate, both hit margin directly
Exception routing by dollar value and customer tier is what turns a doc backlog into managed risk
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, run a sample of 200 BOLs through an OCR + extraction tool and measure accuracy + time saved versus your current manual baseline.

questions.text: How documented are the decision rules your senior dispatchers use to assign loads?

answers.label: 1. Tribal knowledge, top dispatchers just know
2. A few rules in a wiki, mostly out of date
3. Core rules documented, edge cases still tribal
4. Full rule set documented with examples, reviewed quarterly
5. Rules documented + version-controlled, ready to encode into an agent

questions.text: How consistent are routing decisions across dispatchers for similar shipments?

answers.label: 1. Two dispatchers route the same shipment 3 different ways
2. Major decisions consistent, edge cases vary widely
3. Standard playbook followed, exceptions handled differently
4. Tight consistency, variance is intentional based on context
5. Near-zero variance on standard shipments, exceptions documented and reviewed

questions.text: How structured is your decision logic for exception handling (delays, damage, cancellations)?

answers.label: 1. Each exception is handled ad hoc by whoever picks it up
2. Senior dispatchers handle escalations, no playbook
3. Basic playbook by exception type, judgment calls common
4. Detailed playbook with decision trees, ops lead reviews weekly
5. Fully documented decision logic, agent-ready, human-in-the-loop on judgment calls

low.headline: If your best dispatcher can't write it down, you can't encode it
low.text: Decision logic that lives in tribal knowledge will not survive agent automation. Get the rules out of your senior dispatchers' heads before you ask a model to mimic them.
steps: Sit with your top 2 dispatchers for 90 minutes each and capture the rules they use to assign loads
Document the top 10 exception types and the decision tree for each
Version-control the rules in a shared doc, review monthly, flag drift

mid.headline: Rules are documented, consistency is the gap
mid.text: You have a playbook but dispatchers diverge on edge cases. Encode the standard path first, leave the edge cases as routed exceptions.
steps: Audit 50 recent shipments and quantify decision variance across dispatchers
Extend the playbook to cover the top 5 exception types currently handled ad hoc
Set a quarterly review cadence with the dispatch lead to update rules as carriers and customers change

high.headline: Decision logic is ready for an agent
high.text: Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Pilot agent-driven dispatch on a narrow lane (single customer, single mode) with human-in-the-loop review
Track agent decisions versus dispatcher overrides, retrain on the overrides
Expand scope only when override rate drops below 10% on the pilot lane

operator_brief.headline_number: ~12 hrs/week recoverable from consistent routing across dispatchers
operator_brief.lever: Document the top 10 dispatch decisions this quarter and stop letting tribal knowledge gate your AI roadmap.
talking_points: An agent can only mimic decision logic that's already explicit, tribal knowledge is the bottleneck before tooling
Variance across dispatchers on similar shipments is a margin leak, not a quirk
The first agent pilot should be a narrow lane with high-volume + low-variance, not the messiest part of the floor
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, shadow your top dispatcher for 4 hours and capture every routing decision they make, then compare to your written playbook to find the gaps.

questions.text: How API-accessible are your TMS, WMS, and carrier systems?

answers.label: 1. CSV exports and email-based handoffs dominate
2. Partial APIs, heavy reliance on screen scraping for some carriers
3. APIs exist on core systems, carrier coverage is uneven
4. All core systems on stable APIs, tier-1 carriers covered
5. Full API coverage across TMS, WMS, and tier-1/2 carriers, documented and monitored

questions.text: How reliable is your workflow automation layer (n8n, Make, Workato, custom)?

answers.label: 1. No automation platform, everything runs through people or scripts
2. A few Zapier flows, no monitoring or error handling
3. Workflow platform in place, partial coverage, ad hoc maintenance
4. Self-hosted or enterprise platform, monitored, error handling defined
5. Production-grade platform with versioning, monitoring, retry logic, and clear ownership

questions.text: How automated are customer-facing data exchanges (portals, EDI, status webhooks)?

answers.label: 1. Customers call or email for status, ops keys it manually
2. Basic portal with manual updates, EDI for top 1-2 customers only
3. Portal auto-updates, EDI on top 5 customers, gaps on mid-tier
4. Portal + EDI + webhooks across most customers, monitored
5. Fully automated exchanges with all tiered customers, status events flow without human touch

low.headline: Your stack can't talk to itself, agents can't help
low.text: If CSV exports and email handoffs dominate, no agent can move information end-to-end. The integration layer is the wiring AI runs on.
steps: Inventory every system in your stack and mark API coverage: full, partial, none
Stand up n8n (self-hosted) or a comparable platform to start consolidating the manual handoffs
Pick one customer EDI flow to automate first, prove the pattern, expand

mid.headline: Integration coverage is partial, agent reach is limited
mid.text: You have the bones but gaps in carrier coverage and mid-tier customer exchanges will cap what any agent can do.
steps: Close the carrier API gap on tier-2 carriers, screen scraping is technical debt that breaks under load
Add monitoring + retry logic to every workflow, silent failures kill agent trust faster than anything else
Roll EDI or webhook status exchanges to your next 10 customers by revenue

high.headline: Connectivity is agent-ready
high.text: Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add SLA tracking on every workflow and alert on degradation, not just failure
Build a workflow catalog with ownership, version, and rollback path for each
Pilot agent-orchestrated workflows on a narrow lane, measure latency and error budget

operator_brief.headline_number: ~14 hrs/week of manual data movement recoverable from closing integration gaps
operator_brief.lever: Run a stack inventory this month and rank systems by API coverage and business criticality.
talking_points: Screen scraping carriers is hidden technical debt, it works until volume doubles or the carrier updates their portal
A workflow automation platform without monitoring is a future incident waiting to happen, ownership matters more than tool choice
Customer EDI and webhook coverage directly reduces the inbound 'where's my shipment' call volume on ops
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, automate one recurring customer status report end-to-end with n8n or a comparable tool and measure the hours saved versus the ops coordinator's prior baseline.

questions.text: How clearly defined is the human review path for AI or agent outputs that touch customers, carriers, or compliance?

answers.label: 1. No defined review path, outputs ship without a human in the loop
2. Spot-check reviews by whoever has time
3. Defined reviewer per workflow, SLA undefined
4. Reviewer + SLA + escalation path defined per workflow
5. Full review governance with metrics, drift monitoring, and quarterly audit

questions.text: How complete is your audit trail for automated decisions (who decided, what input, what output, what override)?

answers.label: 1. No audit trail, decisions disappear into the system
2. Basic logs, not queryable, scattered across systems
3. Logs centralized but reviewed only on incident
4. Full audit trail per decision, reviewed weekly
5. Audit trail with override tracking and retraining feedback loop

questions.text: How clearly is ownership of each automated workflow defined (who owns it, who fixes it, what SLA)?

answers.label: 1. No defined ownership, breaks get hot-potatoed
2. Informal ownership, depends on who built it
3. Named owner per workflow, no SLA
4. Owner + SLA + backup defined, reviewed quarterly
5. Full RACI per workflow with monitoring, on-call, and quarterly business review

low.headline: Without governance, the first agent failure costs you a customer
low.text: Agents that ship outputs to customers, carriers, or compliance without a defined human review path are an incident waiting to happen. Build governance before the build.
steps: Define the human reviewer for every workflow that touches external parties, full stop
Stand up a basic audit log capturing input, decision, output, and override per automated decision
Assign a named owner to each workflow with SLA on response time when it breaks

mid.headline: Governance exists but it's not load-bearing yet
mid.text: You have reviewers and logs but they're not connected to a feedback loop. That's where override patterns get missed and agent quality drifts unnoticed.
steps: Add weekly review cadence on override rates per workflow, surface drift to ops leadership
Define escalation paths for each workflow when SLAs slip
Build a retraining or rule-update process when override patterns recur

high.headline: Governance is mature, agents can scale safely
high.text: Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Run quarterly audits on agent decisions versus dispatcher overrides, retire workflows that consistently underperform
Publish workflow ownership and SLA externally to customer success and account teams
Add agent confidence scoring to the audit trail and alert when confidence drift exceeds threshold

operator_brief.headline_number: Customer churn risk from one ungoverned agent decision: $50K-$500K per account
operator_brief.lever: Stand up a basic human-in-the-loop review path and audit trail before deploying any agent that touches customers or carriers.
talking_points: 15-20% of agent outputs should route to a human reviewer by design, that's not failure, that's the model working
An ungoverned agent decision that hits a customer wrong is a contract conversation, not a workflow tweak
Audit trail data is what makes future retraining possible, without it, every model update is starting from scratch
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, map every existing automated workflow to a named human reviewer, an SLA, and an escalation path, and surface the gaps to ops leadership.
